item.title: Assign a workspace to a specific Output (Display)
item.description:
i3 and sway can open a workspace on a given output (monitor) every time. To set this up, add workspace ... output ... lines to a config partial: a file in your user config directory that Regolith includes after its own configuration. The variables $ws1 to $ws19 hold the names of Regolith’s workspaces, which you can change as described in Change Workspace Icons and Labels.

X11 Session (i3)

  1. Find the name of the output with xrandr --listmonitors:

    $ xrandr --listmonitors
Monitors: 2
 0: +*eDP-1 1920/309x1080/173+0+0 eDP-1
 1: +HDMI-1 1920/527x1080/296+1920+0 HDMI-1

    The output names are in the last column, here eDP-1 and HDMI-1.

  2. Create a partial, for example ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config.d/70_workspace-outputs, with a line for each workspace:

    ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config.d/70_workspace-outputs
    workspace "$ws1" output eDP-1
workspace "$ws2" output HDMI-1

    Keep the double quotes around the variable: Regolith’s workspace names contain spaces.

  3. Log out and back in, or reload i3 with super shift c.

With regolith-session older than 1.2.2 (Regolith 3.4 and earlier), i3 reports a CONFIG error for these lines right after login (regolith-desktop#890). Refreshing Regolith with super shift r or regolith-look refresh after logging in fixes the workspace names and restarts i3, which then applies the lines.

Wayland Session (sway)

  1. Find the name of the output with swaymsg -t get_outputs:

    $ swaymsg -t get_outputs
Output eDP-1 'AU Optronics 0x573D Unknown' (focused)
[...]
Output HDMI-A-1 'ViewSonic Corporation VG2448 V5E192121969'
[...]

  2. Create a partial, for example ~/.config/regolith3/sway/config.d/70_workspace-outputs, with a line for each workspace:

    ~/.config/regolith3/sway/config.d/70_workspace-outputs
    workspace $ws1 output eDP-1
workspace $ws2 output HDMI-A-1

    Write the variable without quotes here. Regolith’s sway config already quotes $ws1 to $ws19, and with extra quotes the line doesn’t match the workspace.

  3. Log out and back in, or reload sway with super shift c.

Because the two sessions need different quoting, use the i3 and sway partial directories for these lines, not ~/.config/regolith3/common-wm/config.d/.

More Than One Output

A line can list several outputs. The workspace opens on the first of them that is available. With the following line, workspace 2 opens on the external monitor when it is connected, and on the laptop screen otherwise:

~/.config/regolith3/i3/config.d/70_workspace-outputs
workspace "$ws2" output HDMI-1 eDP-1

In sway, the same line is workspace $ws2 output HDMI-A-1 eDP-1.

See the i3 user guide and man 5 sway for details.

item.title: Change background
item.description:
Wallpaper

Most Regolith Looks provide a default desktop color or image. The wallpaper can be set by specifying the path to the wallpaper image via the Xresources key regolith.wallpaper.file. The keys on this page work in both the X11 (i3) and the Wayland (sway) session (Debian 12 has the X11 session only), with the differences listed in Wayland (sway).

You can also pick a wallpaper under Background in the Appearance page of the Regolith Control Center, which can be opened by running regolith-control-center background in the terminal. What it does depends on the release. On Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12 and 13, it writes regolith.wallpaper.file and regolith.lockscreen.wallpaper.file to ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources and refreshes, so the choice stays after regolith-look refresh, also sets the lock screen, and applies in sway too; remove those lines to undo it. On Ubuntu 25.10 and 26.04, it changes only the X11 wallpaper, until the next regolith-look refresh applies the Xresources values again. The Regolith Control Center on Ubuntu 22.04 has no Background panel.

Example, assuming the file /usr/share/backgrounds/warty-final-ubuntu.png is present (it comes with the ubuntu-wallpapers package; on Debian, use /usr/share/images/desktop-base/default from the desktop-base package):

echo "regolith.wallpaper.file: /usr/share/backgrounds/warty-final-ubuntu.png" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

In the above command the property mentioned is set to the /usr/share/backgrounds/warty-final-ubuntu.png change this path to any other that needs to be used.

To change the image treatment (zoom, scale, etc.) of the wallpaper image in the X11 session, set regolith.wallpaper.options. Options are: none, wallpaper, centered, scaled, stretched, zoom, spanned. The default is wallpaper (tiled).

Example:

echo "regolith.wallpaper.options: zoom" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

To specify a color rather than an image use the Xresource key regolith.wallpaper.color.primary. Use the #RRGGBB form, which both sessions understand. Most looks also set a secondary color for a gradient, so clear it to get a solid color:

echo "regolith.wallpaper.file: " >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
echo "regolith.wallpaper.color.primary: #0000FF" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
echo "regolith.wallpaper.color.secondary: " >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

To specify a secondary color and gradient (X11 session only; regolith.wallpaper.color.shading.type is horizontal or vertical):

echo "regolith.wallpaper.file: " >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
echo "regolith.wallpaper.color.primary: #0000FF" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
echo "regolith.wallpaper.color.secondary: #00FF00" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
echo "regolith.wallpaper.color.shading.type: vertical" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

Lockscreen Wallpaper

The lockscreen wallpaper can be managed in the same way as the desktop wallpaper. The keys are the same as desktop wallpaper, but with lockscreen prefixed to wallpaper, like so: regolith.lockscreen.wallpaper.... For example, to specify a lockscreen image:

echo "regolith.lockscreen.wallpaper.file: /usr/share/backgrounds/warty-final-ubuntu.png" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

Disable Wallpaper handling

If you wish to manage wallpaper externally to Regolith in the X11 session, simply specify empty values for wallpaper image and color:

echo "regolith.wallpaper.file: " >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
echo "regolith.wallpaper.color.primary: " >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources

In the Wayland session this leaves a black background instead; see below.

Wayland (sway)

Debian 12 has no Wayland session, so this section applies to the other releases. In sway the wallpaper is drawn by swaybg, which Regolith starts from regolith.wallpaper.file and regolith.wallpaper.color.primary each time the session starts or regolith-look refresh runs. The differences from X11 are:

  • Image placement: regolith.wallpaper.options is not used. Set regolith.wallpaper.mode instead, to one of stretch, fill, fit, center or tile. The default is fill.

    echo "regolith.wallpaper.mode: fit" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

  • Colors: regolith.wallpaper.color.primary must be in the #RRGGBB form. sway rejects color names such as blue, and no wallpaper is drawn, even when an image is set (sway shows its default background: black on newer sway, dark grey on Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04). The secondary color and the shading type are not used, so the color is always solid.

  • Lock screen: the lock screen (gtklock) shows regolith.lockscreen.wallpaper.file. The lockscreen color keys are not used.

  • Settings: on Ubuntu 25.10 and 26.04, picking a wallpaper under Background in the Appearance page of the Regolith Control Center does not change the sway wallpaper. Use the Xresources keys.

  • Managing the wallpaper yourself: empty values give a black background, because Regolith still sets one. Remove the package that sets it, then set the wallpaper in your own sway config partial:

    sudo apt remove regolith-sway-background
mkdir -p ~/.config/regolith3/sway/config.d
echo "output * bg /usr/share/backgrounds/warty-final-ubuntu.png fill" > ~/.config/regolith3/sway/config.d/90_wallpaper
swaymsg reload

item.title: Change Bar Status indicators
item.description:
The X11 session (i3) and the Wayland session (sway) use different status bar programs:

  • X11: i3xrocks. Each status indicator is a separate i3xrocks-* package.
  • Wayland: i3status-rs, configured by a single file. The i3xrocks-* packages have no effect there; see Wayland (sway) below.

Adding or Removing status indicators

Finding Status Indicators 

apt search i3xrocks-

Installing a Status Indicator 

sudo apt install i3xrocks-memory
regolith-look refresh

To remove an indicator, remove its package (for example sudo apt remove i3xrocks-memory) and run regolith-look refresh.

Customization of the i3 bar

Each status indicator on the bar is managed by a file. The name of the file maps to the position of the status indicator on the bar, e.g. a file’s name starting with 10_ mean its corresponding indicator will be positioned before an indicator which has a configuration file starting with 20_. Within each file there is some information that i3xrocks uses to execute a script that ultimately returns the data you see on the bar. Some of the status indicators have configuration parameters that can be adjusted to your liking. For example, if you would prefer that the battery status changes more frequently, the polling interval can be updated. The first thing to do in order to customize the bar is to copy the indicators you wish to see from /usr/share/i3xrocks/conf.d/ to ~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d. Each file in ~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d can be modified as you see fit. To change the order of status indicators on the bar, simply change the name of the files to the sort order you prefer.

Once you’ve made your changes, refreshing the session should cause the bar to update based on your new configuration.

For example, to show the CPU indicator before the network traffic indicator and not display the memory indicator, perform the following steps (the files in /usr/share/i3xrocks/conf.d/ depend on the indicator packages you have installed):

$ ls /usr/share/i3xrocks/conf.d/
01_setup
30_net-traffic
40_cpu-usage
50_memory
90_time
$ mkdir -p ~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d
$ cp /usr/share/i3xrocks/conf.d/01_setup ~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d/01_setup
$ cp /usr/share/i3xrocks/conf.d/40_cpu-usage ~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d/20_cpu-usage
$ cp /usr/share/i3xrocks/conf.d/30_net-traffic ~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d/30_net-traffic
$ cp /usr/share/i3xrocks/conf.d/90_time ~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d/90_time
$ regolith-look refresh

In the above steps the following actions are performed:

  • The current i3xrocks modules are listed that exist in the directory created by regolith
  • The directory where user configuration lives is created at ~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d
  • Four files are copied from the application created directory to the user created directory. 01_setup holds the settings shared by all indicators, so keep it. Renaming 40_cpu-usage to 20_cpu-usage moves the CPU indicator in front of the network traffic indicator, and the memory indicator is not copied, so it is not shown
  • The regolith-look refresh command is run to refresh the Bar Status Indicators

Note: If the directory ~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d exists, the defaults in /usr/share/i3xrocks/conf.d/ are ignored, even if the directory is empty. Copy every indicator you want to keep, and remove the directory to go back to the defaults. Indicator packages you install later are not added to the bar until you copy their file as well.

Wayland (sway)

The sway bar runs i3status-rs with /etc/regolith/i3status-rust/config.toml. To change the indicators, copy that file, edit the copy, and point the Xresource wm.bar.status_config at it:

mkdir -p ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust
cp /etc/regolith/i3status-rust/config.toml ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml
echo "wm.bar.status_config: ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources

Each [[block]] section in the file is one indicator, shown in the order of the file. Remove a section to hide an indicator, move it to change the order, or add a block, for example the CPU indicator:

~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml
[[block]]
block = "cpu"

Then run regolith-look refresh. The available blocks and their options are described in the i3status-rust documentation.

Further Reading

The reference page for configurations has more details about the configuration files used with Regolith Linux.

item.title: Change Notification Systems
item.description:
Regolith ships with a notification system called Rofication. It is designed to work in the background and not use pop-ups as a way of alerting the user to a new notification. Rather, a bar item displays the current number of unread notifications and a dialog, opened with super n, lists the current notifications. This page describes a way to install an alternative notification system which works in a more traditional way.

We will use dunst as an example, because it works in both the X11 (i3) and the Wayland (sway) session. Similar steps can be used with other notification components; see Other Notification Daemons below.

  1. Replace Rofication with dunst:

    sudo apt install dunst libnotify-bin

    dunst conflicts with Rofication, so apt also removes regolith-rofication and regolith-wm-rofication-ilia, the package that starts Rofication and binds super n to its dialog. If you want to remove the remaining configuration, the following works as well:

    sudo apt purge regolith-rofication # remove any remaining config as well

  2. Log out and back in.

  3. Test your notifications with notify-send test123. You should see a pop-up notification from dunst.

D-Bus starts dunst when the first notification arrives. To configure it, see man dunst and man 5 dunst; your own settings go in ~/.config/dunst/dunstrc.

Sway: Notification Count in the Bar

In the Wayland session, after Rofication is removed, the bar can show a red Failed to connect to socket where the notification count was. Until your i3status-rs package hides this block by itself, use your own copy of the bar configuration without it:

  1. Copy the default configuration:

    mkdir -p ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust
cp /etc/regolith/i3status-rust/config.toml ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml

  2. In the copy, delete the [[block]] entry with block = "rofication" and the [[block.click]] lines that follow it.

  3. Tell the bar to use your copy, and reload:

    echo "wm.bar.status_config: ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

Other Notification Daemons

Daemon Package X11 (i3) Wayland (sway)
dunst dunst yes yes
mako mako-notifier no yes
SwayNotificationCenter sway-notification-center no yes

mako and SwayNotificationCenter don’t conflict with Rofication, so apt leaves it installed, and Rofication keeps receiving the notifications. Remove it yourself:

sudo apt remove regolith-rofication regolith-wm-rofication-ilia

Both only run in the Wayland session. If one of them is your only notification daemon, the X11 session shows no notifications.

Going Back to Rofication 

sudo apt install regolith-rofication regolith-wm-rofication-ilia

This removes dunst. Log out and back in.

item.title: Change the Bar Date and Time Format
item.description:
The X11 (i3) and Wayland (sway) sessions use different bars, which are configured differently.

X11 Session (i3)

The time format (12 or 24 hour) can be specified in Settings, under System > Date & Time > Time Format. The bar picks up the change within about ten seconds.

The order of day and month follows the country of your LC_TIME locale: month first (MM/DD) for the United States, Canada, China, Japan and a few other countries, and day first (DD/MM) for all others.

The date and time formats can also be explicitly set via Xresources. To do so, override the i3xrocks.date.format2 Xresource key in ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources. The value is the format that would be passed to the date command on the command line, without the leading +. For example, the following line uses the YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm format:

~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
i3xrocks.date.format2: %Y-%m-%d %H:%M

Then run regolith-look refresh. The bar shows the date and time like this:

While this key is set, the bar no longer follows the Time Format setting.

The most useful formats that are supported are as follows:

  • %Y prints year as YYYY
  • %y prints year as YY
  • %m prints month as MM
  • %d prints day as DD
  • %H prints hours in 24 hour format
  • %I prints hours in 12 hour format
  • %M prints minute as mm
  • %p prints AM or PM

For more details and placeholders, please look at date --help.

Wayland Session (sway)

The sway bar, i3status-rs, doesn’t read i3xrocks.date.format2 or the Time Format setting. Its date and time formats are part of its configuration file. To change them, use your own copy of that file:

  1. Copy the default configuration:

    mkdir -p ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust
cp /etc/regolith/i3status-rust/config.toml ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml

  2. In the copy, change the format of the two time blocks. By default, the date block uses %a-%d/%m/%y and the time block uses %R (24 hour hh:mm). For example, for YYYY-MM-DD and a 12 hour clock:

    ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml
    [[block]]
block = "time"
interval = 5
format = "\uf073 $timestamp.datetime(f:'%Y-%m-%d')"

[[block]]
block = "time"
interval = 5
format = "$icon $timestamp.datetime(f:'%I:%M %p')"

    On Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian, the file has a single time block with a plain format, format = "%d/%m %R"; change that one instead.

  3. Tell the bar to use your copy, and reload:

    echo "wm.bar.status_config: ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

    With the example above, the bar shows the date and time like this:

The placeholders are the same as for date, listed above. See the time block documentation for the other options.

item.title: Change the Default Terminal
item.description:
The terminal keybinding, super enter, runs x-terminal-emulator, which is gnome-terminal by default. Any terminal emulator can be used instead. Both methods below change the terminal of the X11 (i3) and the Wayland (sway) session alike. A Wayland-only terminal such as foot does not start in the X11 session, so choose one that runs in both unless you only use the Wayland session.

For all users

To update Regolith to use your already installed terminal of your choice, use update-alternatives to specify it as default:

  1. Run sudo update-alternatives --config x-terminal-emulator to see all available terminals installed on your system.
  2. Type the number of the terminal you prefer and press Enter.

For your user only

Set the Xresource wm.program.terminal to the terminal command, then refresh the session. For example, for alacritty:

echo "wm.program.terminal: /usr/bin/alacritty" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

item.title: Change the Default Window Gap
item.description:
Regolith version 3.0 onward replaces “i3-wm” with “wm” in Xresource keys. The content on this page has been updated for Regolith 3.0+. If you are using an earlier version, use “i3-wm” instead of “wm” in the key names below. For example wm.foo.bar changes to i3-wm.foo.bar for Regolith 1.x and 2.x.

Like most configuration in Regolith, the i3-gaps gap size can be tuned via Xresources (See here for all Xresource definitions).

  1. Create or add the following value to your ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources file:
~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
wm.gaps.inner.size: 20

In this example we’re setting the default gap to 20 pixels.

  1. Reload the Xresources configuration:
regolith-look refresh

Further Reading

See the reference page for configurations for more details about config files in Regolith.

item.title: Change the lock screen program
item.description:
The X11 session (i3) and the Wayland session (sway) lock the screen with different programs, so they are configured separately.

X11 session

Configure gnome-flashback to Disable Built-in Lockscreen

By default gnome-flashback handles the lock screen in the X11 session. This can be adjusted by modifying its configuration via the gsettings command line program:

gsettings set org.gnome.gnome-flashback screensaver false

gnome-flashback also locks the screen when the session is idle and before the computer suspends. With its lock screen disabled, these locks no longer happen; set them up yourself if you need them (for example with xss-lock).

Cause Your Lock screen program to Run from i3 Keybinding

Specify the following override line in your ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources file (substituting your-script.sh with the command you wish to use for the locking your screen):

Regolith 3.4 replaced the key wm.program.lock with wm.program.lock_i3 for the X11 session and wm.program.lock_sway for the Wayland session. On Regolith 3.0 to 3.3, use wm.program.lock. Regolith 1.x and 2.x use i3-wm.program.lock.
~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
wm.program.lock_i3: your-script.sh

For example, assuming you have i3lock installed:

echo "wm.program.lock_i3: /usr/bin/i3lock" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

The lock screen keybinding, super escape, then runs i3lock.

Wayland session

The Wayland session locks the screen with gtklock. The Xresource wm.program.lock_sway sets the lock command. It is used for the lock screen keybinding, after the session has been idle, before the computer suspends, and when the lid is closed. The command must return once the screen is locked, so start the locker in the background (for example swaylock -f or gtklock -d):

sudo apt install swaylock
echo "wm.program.lock_sway: swaylock -f -c 000000" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

The gsettings command above has no effect in the Wayland session.

item.title: Change the Terminal Font Size
item.description:
Regolith sets the font of its GNOME Terminal profile, named “Regolith”, from the gnome.terminal.font Xresources key. By default, this is the monospace font of the current look. The steps are the same in the X11 (i3) and Wayland (sway) sessions.

  1. Look up the current value with xrescat gnome.terminal.font in the X11 session, or trawlcat gnome.terminal.font in the Wayland session. With the default look, it is BitstreamVeraSansMono Nerd Font 12.

  2. Create or add the following value to your ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources file, with the font name and the size you want. For example, the default font in size 14:

~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
gnome.terminal.font: BitstreamVeraSansMono Nerd Font 14

To use another font, install it first. For example, after sudo apt install fonts-jetbrains-mono you can use JetBrains Mono 14. fc-list : family lists the names of the installed fonts.

  1. Reload the Xresources configuration:
regolith-look refresh

The Regolith profile is updated, and open GNOME Terminal windows change to the new font.

This only applies to GNOME Terminal. If you use another terminal, set the font in that terminal’s own configuration. To stop Regolith from changing the GNOME Terminal profile at all, set gnome.terminal.update: false.

item.title: Change Workspace Icons and Labels
item.description:
Adding icons to workspaces can give your desktop a nice and functional look. The steps on this page work in both the X11 (i3) and the Wayland (sway) session.

Finding icons

Icons are actually characters from fonts installed by Regolith looks. Every look uses a Nerd Font for the bar, which contains thousands of icons. The bar font is set by the Xresource wm.bar.font; you can see the current one with xrescat wm.bar.font in the X11 session or trawlcat wm.bar.font in the Wayland session. For example, the default look uses BitstromWera Nerd Font (BitstreamVeraSansMono Nerd Font in Regolith 3.4 and earlier).

You can browse the icons on the Nerd Fonts cheat sheet, or in the font itself using the GNOME Character Map application from the gucharmap package.

The cheat sheet lists Nerd Fonts 3 code points. Regolith 3.5 and later ship Nerd Fonts 3, so any icon on it works. Regolith 3.4 and earlier ship Nerd Fonts 2.1.0, which doesn’t have the cheat sheet’s Material Design icons (nf-md-*, code points U+F0001 and above): they show as boxes. On those releases, use an icon from another set, such as nf-fa-*, or pick it from the font itself with Character Map.

Nerd Fonts 3 also removed the old Material Design icons (nf-mdi-*, U+F500 to U+FD46). If your workspace names use them, they show as boxes after upgrading to Regolith 3.5: replace each with the matching nf-md-* icon. See the 3.5 release notes.

To pick an icon with Character Map:

  1. Open “Character Map”.
  2. Select your icon font in the top left combo.
  3. In the script pane select Common.
  4. Scroll down the characters pane until you find the icons.
  5. Double click on the icon you are looking to use and press the Copy button (bottom right).

Tip: the icons are in the Unicode private use areas, starting at U+E000. In Nerd Fonts 3 the Material Design icons are in the supplementary private use area, starting at U+F0001.

Changing Icons

Follow these steps to override the default workspace label with your own:

  1. Find the character you want to use and copy to the clipboard. This example will use the terminal glyph (U+F120, nf-fa-terminal on the cheat sheet): 
  2. Add a line to your Xresources overrides file with the workspace number and character you wish to use:
Regolith version 3.0 onward replaces “i3-wm” with “wm” in Xresource keys. The content on this page has been updated for Regolith 3.0+. If you are using an earlier version, use “i3-wm” instead of “wm” in the key names below. For example wm.foo.bar changes to i3-wm.foo.bar for Regolith 1.x and 2.x.
echo "wm.workspace.06.name: 6:" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
  1. Refresh your UI:
regolith-look refresh

Workspace labels are only updated when a workspace is created. Ensure you’re creating a new workspace 6 if following the example above, for example with super 6 while workspace 6 does not exist.

Changing Labels

The same approach can be used to specify textual descriptions of your workspaces. For example, adding the following lines to your ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources file will change the first three workspaces:

~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
wm.workspace.01.name: 1: Terminal
wm.workspace.02.name: 2: Web
wm.workspace.03.name: 3: Chat

Keep the number and the colon at the start of each name: the workspace keybindings find workspaces by that number, and the bar hides it.

With these three labels and the terminal glyph on workspace 6, the bar shows the workspaces like this, in the X11 session (top) and in the Wayland session (bottom):

Further Reading

See the reference page for configurations for more details about config files in Regolith.

item.title: Disable Mouse Hiding (unclutter)
item.description:
By default the mouse cursor disappears if unused for a few seconds. If you prefer that the mouse cursor always remains visible on the screen, follow the steps for your session.

X11 session

In the X11 session (i3), unclutter-xfixes hides the cursor.

  1. Specify an empty value for the unclutter launcher program with an Xresources override:
echo "wm.program.unclutter: :" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
  1. Log out and back in for changes to take effect.

Alternatively, remove the package that starts it with sudo apt remove regolith-i3-unclutter, then log out and back in.

Wayland session

In the Wayland session, sway hides the cursor after 5 seconds without movement, and also while you type. To turn off both:

  1. Add these Xresources overrides (a timeout of 0 turns off hiding):
echo "wm.hide_cursor.timout: 0" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
echo "wm.hide_cursor.show_when_typing: disable" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
  1. Run regolith-look refresh.

Alternatively, remove the package that sets this up with sudo apt remove regolith-sway-unclutter, then log out and back in.

The key is spelled timout, as in the Regolith configuration. Set wm.hide_cursor.timout to another value in milliseconds to change the delay instead.

item.title: Find and Install Packages
item.description:
Regolith is a Debian-based system. Debian packaging tools can be used to find and install packages.

Find package via the command line

The apt command can be used to query installed or all packages:

apt list --installed <package name> # finds installed packages
apt list <package name> # finds all packages

For example, to list all official Regolith looks that could be installed, run:

$ apt list 'regolith-look-*'
...

Quote patterns such as regolith-look-* so that the shell does not expand them to file names first.

To see which status indicators are installed on your system, run:

apt list --installed 'i3xrocks-*'

The i3xrocks-* status indicators are used by the bar of the X11 session. The bar of the Wayland session uses i3status-rs, whose blocks are configured in a file rather than installed as packages. See Install the Sway Compositor.

Install packages via the command line

To install packages via the command line, again we can us the apt command, but must use sudo to gain the rights necessary for installation:

sudo apt install <package name>

To install the battery status indicator, run:

sudo apt install i3xrocks-battery

New status indicators appear on the bar after regolith-look refresh or the next login, unless you have staged your own i3xrocks configuration. In that case, copy the indicator’s file from /usr/share/i3xrocks/conf.d/ as well.

Find and Install Packages via GUI app

There are a number of apps that can provide a nice window interface on top of the apt packaging system, for example synaptic. Refer to the documentation for the tool of your choice to learn how to search for and install packages.

item.title: Customize Compositor
item.description:
Pay special attention to this section if you are experiencing odd visual glitches or slow graphics performance.

A compositor is a UI component that applies visual effects to windows before they are rendered on-screen. Many desktop environments integrate a compositor directly into the window manager, making it difficult to switch out or disable. In Regolith, the compositor is defined as a pluggable “extension point” in the packaging system. This means that compositors can be switched out simply by installing the packages that contain them. The underlying packaging system will ensure there are no conflicts and that all the dependencies of a given compositor are also installed.

This page applies to the X11 session (i3) only. In the Wayland session, sway is itself the compositor, and the regolith-compositor-* packages have no effect.
Since Regolith 3.0, the default compositor of the X11 session is Picom (regolith-compositor-picom-glx). In Regolith 2.x, the default was “no compositor”; in Regolith 1.x, it was Picom.

Finding available compositors

The following command will list all compositors configured to work with Regolith:

apt search regolith-compositor-

You should find at least the following:

  • regolith-compositor-picom-glx [default]: Uses picom. Recommended for most users to resolve screen tearing and add visual effects. Modern and well-maintained fork of compton.
  • regolith-compositor-none: No compositor. Best performance, no visual effects.
  • regolith-compositor-compton-glx: An ancestor of picom which is no longer maintained.
  • regolith-compositor-xcompmgr: An early compositor that may offer more consistent performance if more complex compositors are problematic.

Installing a compositor

Due to the way that the compositor is managed by i3-wm, you must log out and back in for compositor changes to take effect. Restarting i3 is not sufficient.

Run the following package install command to swap out the compositor. In this case we’ll install picom:

sudo apt install regolith-compositor-picom-glx

To run without a compositor, install regolith-compositor-none the same way.

Log out and then log back in and the new compositor should be loaded. You can verify by checking the process list for picom:

pgrep -a picom

Overriding Regolith default compositor configuration

Picom

To provide your own Picom compositor config, copy the default or create your own and save it as ~/.config/regolith3/picom/config. It is loaded instead of the default config /etc/regolith/picom/config the next time i3 starts, so regolith-look refresh (which restarts i3) applies it without logging out:

mkdir -p ~/.config/regolith3/picom
cp /etc/regolith/picom/config ~/.config/regolith3/picom/config

Some looks ship their own Picom config and select it with the Xresource regolith.compositor.picom.config. A file in ~/.config/regolith3/picom/config takes precedence over it.

If the screen stops updating in the X11 session (new windows do not appear and workspace switches do not show), for example in a virtual machine without 3D acceleration, Picom’s glx backend may not work with software rendering. Set backend = "xrender"; in your config, or use regolith-compositor-none.

Compton

regolith-compositor-compton-glx reads ~/.config/regolith3/compton/config instead of its default config /etc/regolith/compton/config.

item.title: Customize i3 Configuration
item.description:
The root configuration is /etc/regolith/i3/config. It loads the default configuration partials, first those shared with the Wayland session in /usr/share/regolith/common/config.d, then the i3-only ones in /usr/share/regolith/i3/config.d, each directory in alphabetical order. Then user configurations in ~/.config/regolith3/common-wm/config.d (shared with the Wayland session) and ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config.d are loaded, also in alphabetical order. Regolith’s default configuration is built to be customized by setting Xresources variables, adding user configuration, and adding or removing default configurations via apt. For this reason, there are several approaches to customization of i3 in Regolith that can be used separately or in combination to achieve your configuration cleanly:

  • Use Xresources to override variables, e.g. keybindings, strings, program names, colors, etc.
  • Add or remove Regolith default configuration files with apt
  • Add your own user configuration files
  • Replace Regolith’s configuration wholesale

How to set an Xresources variable

The following configuration example (from /usr/share/regolith/i3/config.d/80_compositor) can be customized to load whatever compositor you want, without editing or overriding the existing i3 configuration file, by setting $wm.program.compositor.

Regolith version 3.0 onward replaces “i3-wm” with “wm” in Xresource keys. The content on this page has been updated for Regolith 3.0+. If you are using an earlier version, use “i3-wm” instead of “wm” in the key names below. For example wm.foo.bar changes to i3-wm.foo.bar for Regolith 1.x and 2.x.
/usr/share/regolith/i3/config.d/80_compositor
set_from_resource $wm.program.compositor wm.program.compositor /usr/share/regolith-compositor/init
exec_always --no-startup-id $wm.program.compositor

To do this, simply add a line to ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources like:

~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
# Use my own home-made compositor
wm.program.compositor: /usr/local/bin/my-compositor

Similarly, you can override other i3 options with Xresources based on the variable names found in the /usr/share/regolith/common/config.d and /usr/share/regolith/i3/config.d files:

~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
## Gap configuration
wm.gaps.inner.size: 1

## Border configuration
wm.window.border.size: 3
wm.client.focused.color.child_border: #AAD3E9

## Workspace names
wm.workspace.01.name: 1:FOO

For more, please read a more in-depth discussion on Xresources

How to uninstall a default partial

If you want to wholly replace or remove settings provided by a default partial, you can use apt to remove the package which provides that partial.

To identify the name of the package that provides the partial you want to remove:

dpkg -S /usr/share/regolith/common/config.d/40_workspace-config

The output contains the name of the package:

regolith-wm-workspace-config: /usr/share/regolith/common/config.d/40_workspace-config

Validate the full list of files provided by this package so you know what you’re removing:

dpkg -L regolith-wm-workspace-config

Remove the partial:

sudo apt remove regolith-wm-workspace-config

How to customize a default partial

To customize only one of Regolith’s default partials, you must first ensure that the file ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config does not exist. This overrides Regolith’s defaults entirely, which is incompatible with this how-to.

First, ensure that a directory exists for user config partials.

mkdir -p ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config.d

Then, copy the default configuration into your user configuration directory:

cp /usr/share/regolith/common/config.d/40_workspace-config ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config.d/

Make your desired changes:

vim ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config.d/40_workspace-config

Clean up the package containing the defaults:

sudo apt remove regolith-wm-workspace-config

Finally, restart i3 or log out and back in.

40_workspace-config comes from /usr/share/regolith/common/config.d, so the Wayland session loads it too, and removing its package removes it from both sessions. To keep your copy in both sessions, put it in ~/.config/regolith3/common-wm/config.d/ instead of ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config.d/.

Change Regolith’s defaults outside of Xresources options

If you need more configuration than the above article provides please visit Staging Config Files

How to replace Regolith’s defaults completely

If you don’t want to keep any of Regolith’s defaults (for example, you’re an experienced i3 user with a complete personal config you want to use), you can either uninstall all of Regolith’s config partials, and/or create your own root config at ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config.

Wayland (sway) session

The Wayland session works the same way, with these paths:

  • Root configuration: /etc/regolith/sway/config, replaced by ~/.config/regolith3/sway/config if that file exists.
  • Default partials: /usr/share/regolith/common/config.d (shared with i3) and /usr/share/regolith/sway/config.d.
  • User partials: ~/.config/regolith3/common-wm/config.d (shared with i3) and ~/.config/regolith3/sway/config.d.

Most Xresources keys apply to both sessions. After a change, run regolith-look refresh or swaymsg reload.

item.title: How to Hide i3-bar by default
item.description:
Regolith version 3.0 onward replaces “i3-wm” with “wm” in Xresource keys. The content on this page has been updated for Regolith 3.0+. If you are using an earlier version, use “i3-wm” instead of “wm” in the key names below. For example wm.foo.bar changes to i3-wm.foo.bar for Regolith 1.x and 2.x.

Add the line

~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
wm.bar.mode: hide

to $HOME/.config/regolith3/Xresources file. The next time you log in the bar should be hidden by default.

item.title: Install the Sway Compositor
item.description:
To install the wayland session, follow these steps:

  1. Install the regolith-session-sway package and its dependencies, which include Regolith’s build of Sway (sway-regolith):

    sudo apt install regolith-session-sway

  2. Log out, or reboot.

  3. Select the “Regolith / Wayland” session in the login panel. In GDM, select your user and choose the session from the gear button in the lower-right corner.

The X11 session (“Regolith / X11”) stays installed, and you can choose either session at each login.

Debian 12 (Bookworm) has the X11 session only. The Wayland session needs Debian 13 (Trixie) or a supported Ubuntu release.

Hardware Support

Those using proprietary nvidia drivers for their graphics cards must set regolith.sway.unsupported_gpu: true in ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources. This is not an issue with the open source drivers nouveau. See more here.

Bar Changes

The wayland session uses i3status-rs rather than i3xrocks. i3status-rs provides a crisper and more resource-efficient approach to system monitoring. However at this time the i3xrocks packages for status indicators are not integrated with i3status-rs. To use a custom configuration with i3status-rs, copy the default configuration to a location of your choosing and set wm.bar.status_config to the path of your copy in ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources:

mkdir -p ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust
cp /etc/regolith/i3status-rust/config.toml ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml
echo "wm.bar.status_config: ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources

Then edit the copy, and run regolith-look refresh or log back in. See the upstream project documentation for further details.

item.title: Launch an app in a Floating Window
item.description:
Most X11 applications support a flag --class to specify the class under which the application runs. Regolith is configured such that apps with a class of floating_window will launch with i3’s floating window mode.

Examples

Firefox

Launch Firefox in floating mode:

firefox --class=floating_window

Alacritty

Launch the Alacritty terminal in floating mode:

alacritty --class floating_window

gnome-terminal

GNOME Terminal ignores --class: its windows are created by a shared gnome-terminal-server process, so they keep the class Gnome-terminal. To float all GNOME Terminal windows instead, add a file to ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config.d/ (see Customize i3 Configuration) with the line for_window [class="Gnome-terminal"] floating enable, and reload i3 with super shift c.

Sway

In the Wayland session the floating_window rule matches only X11 applications that run through XWayland. Native Wayland applications have an app_id instead of a class. To float them, add a rule for that app_id in ~/.config/regolith3/sway/config.d/:

~/.config/regolith3/sway/config.d/80_floating_window
for_window [app_id="floating_window"] floating enable

Then reload Sway with super shift c and set the app_id when launching the application:

alacritty --class floating_window
firefox --name floating_window

swaymsg -t get_tree shows the app_id of open windows.

item.title: Minimal Ubuntu Install
item.description:
This page describes how to install the Regolith Desktop into Ubuntu Server. This approach produces a minimal setup as many of the standard GNOME desktop packages present in a desktop install will be avoided.

Steps

Install Ubuntu Server

Follow online instructions for installing a fresh copy of Ubuntu Server, in a release that Regolith supports. See the Compatibility Matrix.

Add Regolith’s package key and apt repository

Once Ubuntu Server has been installed, log into a terminal session. Register the Regolith public key and add the repository URL for your release, as described in the first two steps of the Install page. The same directions are available as text files:

Ubuntu 25.10 (Questing): install-release-ubuntu-25.10-amd64.txt
Ubuntu 25.04 (Plucky): install-release-ubuntu-25.04-amd64.txt
Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (Noble): install-release-ubuntu-24.04-amd64.txt
Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy): install-release-ubuntu-22.04-amd64.txt

Example:

wget https://regolith-desktop.com/install-release-ubuntu-24.04-amd64.txt
cat install-release-ubuntu-24.04-amd64.txt

Manually execute each step in the text file, or source the file if you’re feeling adventurous. Once complete, the Regolith Desktop package repositories are installed into the new system.

Install the Regolith Ubuntu System

There is a special package that is used in the ISO that can also be used in a minimal install such as this: regolith-system-ubuntu. This package includes extra branding not used in typical desktop installs which may share multiple desktop environments. Run the following command to install Regolith Desktop and all of it’s dependencies:

sudo apt install regolith-system-ubuntu

This installs the X11 session (regolith-session-flashback) and the lightdm login manager. Some recommended packages also bring in gdm3 and GNOME Shell, so apt asks which display manager to use by default: choose lightdm. If you don’t want gdm3 and GNOME Shell, you can remove them afterwards with sudo apt remove gdm3 gnome-shell.

To also install the Wayland session, run:

sudo apt install regolith-session-sway

Reboot

Once the system boots back up, the lightdm login manager will allow you to log into your new Regolith environment.

item.title: Override Xresources
item.description:
Regolith relies on the Xresources system to provide a consolidated interface configuration. By changing Xresources values, Regolith can be customized in ways such as updating the user interface, specifying custom behaviors, or defining a specific format for some of the blocklets on the bar.

In Regolith, Xresources values can be changed via two methods: supplying your own Xresources files, and overriding the existing Xresources values. The latter approach is strongly recommended, as it makes upgrading to newer versions of Regolith less likely to break your customizations. If you copy the Xresources tree completely you’ll need to integrate any breaking changes in future versions manually.

Initialization

When a Regolith session is started, Xresources are loaded in the following order. Later files override values from earlier ones:

File Optional Notes
~/.Xresources Y Intended for non-Regolith settings
~/.config/regolith3/Xresources Y Loaded first so that it can select the look with regolith.look.path
/usr/share/regolith-look/<look>/root N The Regolith Xresources associated with the selected look (regolith-look set), or with the most recently installed look if none is selected
~/.config/regolith3/Xresources Y Loaded again, so that your overrides take precedence over the look

It is recommended to use ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources for customization as it doesn’t require the specification of redundant settings and is easier to maintain over time. It may #include files from ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources.d.

In the X11 session the values are loaded into the X server with xrdb. In the Wayland (Sway) session the same files are loaded, in the same order, into the trawl configuration daemon instead.

Determining which values can be changed

The xrdb tool can be used to list the existing Xresources values in the X11 session. There is a number of existing overrides:

$ xrdb -query
[...]
gtk.document_font_name: Sans 11
gtk.font_name: Bitstream Vera Sans 11
gtk.icon_theme_name: hicolor
gtk.monospace_font_name: BitstreamVeraSansMono Nerd Font 12
gtk.theme_name: Adwaita-dark
wm.bar.background.color: #393939
[...]

In the Wayland session, xrdb -query shows nothing. Use trawldb --query instead, or trawlcat <key> to read a single value:

$ trawldb --query wm.bar.position
wm.bar.position : bottom

Examples

Note that the commands presented below append text to a file, so running the command more than once will result in duplicate entries.

Example - Update the UI for High DPI Screens

By using the ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources override file, we will only need to specify the values we wish to change. The xrdb tool can be used to determine what current values are set to.

  1. Create or add the following value to your ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources file:
~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
Xft.dpi: 192
  1. Reload the Xresources configuration:
regolith-look refresh
  1. Open a new terminal to see the change take effect.

192 is just an example value, please adjust as needed.

Xft.dpi applies to the X11 session only. In the Wayland session, scale the output instead, for example with a file in ~/.config/regolith3/sway/config.d/ containing output * scale 2.

Example - Change i3 bar position 

$ xrdb -query | grep position # trawldb --query wm.bar.position in the Wayland session
wm.bar.position: bottom
$ echo "wm.bar.position: top" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
$ regolith-look refresh

Example - Change GTK Theme 

$ xrdb -query | grep gtk.theme_name
gtk.theme_name: Adwaita-dark
$ echo "gtk.theme_name: Adwaita" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
$ regolith-look refresh

Example - Disable the System Tray 

echo "wm.bar.trayoutput: none" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

This setting applies to the X11 session only.

Example - Use Alt instead of Win as Super 

echo "wm.mod: Mod1" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
echo "wm.alt: Mod4" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
echo "wm.carry_container_to_ws_key: Mod4" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
regolith-look refresh

The third line keeps the “Carry Window to Workspace” bindings on super alt after the swap. Without it, Regolith 3.4 and earlier give “Duplicate keybinding” errors, because the default for that binding is fixed to Mod1. In the Wayland session of those releases, the keyboard layout bindings also use a fixed Mod1, so after the swap alt backspace switches the keyboard layout instead of toggling the split orientation.

Reloading i3 alone does not read the file again: run regolith-look refresh as above, or log back into the session. Some settings may require logging back into the session, for example anything that i3 launches as a separate process.

Further Reading

See the reference page for configurations for more details about config files in Regolith.

item.title: Remove Unneeded Dependencies
item.description:
When Regolith is installed via ISO, only the necessary desktop components or packages are installed by default. However when installing Regolith into an existing Ubuntu system, some desktop components that Regolith does not require will still be installed on the system. There is nothing wrong with keeping these additional packages, in fact they are important if you wish to switch back to the default Ubuntu session at some point, however some users prefer to remove them.

Removing packages may cause unexpected behavior or loss of functionality.

Install LightDM

The lightdm display manager can be installed by with a variety of themes, but we’ll install the package regolith-lightdm-config:

sudo apt install regolith-lightdm-config

Inspect the output of apt to verify you approve of the package changes. When presented with a menu, choosing between gdm3 and lightdm, select lightdm.

Remove Unneeded Packages

Now that we are using the lightdm display manager, we can remove the unneeded packages:

sudo apt remove gdm3 gnome-shell 'evolution-data-server*'

Inspect the output of apt to verify you approve of the package changes.

The Regolith sessions need gnome-session-common, but on Ubuntu 26.04 no remaining package depends on it, so apt autoremove would remove it and logging in would fail. Mark it as manually installed first:

sudo apt-mark manual gnome-session-common

Now we can remove all of the dependencies of those packages:

sudo apt autoremove

If logging in returns you to the login screen after this step, switch to a text console with ctrl alt f3, log in there and run sudo apt install gnome-session-common.

Reboot

At this point the unneeded dependencies have been removed from the system. Reboot to complete the procedure.

Undo

If you decide that you’d like to restore the existing setup, run the following and select gdm3 as the display manager.

sudo apt install gdm3 gnome-shell evolution-data-server ubuntu-session
sudo apt remove regolith-lightdm-config

lightdm itself stays installed. Once gdm3 is the default display manager, you can remove it with sudo apt remove lightdm.

item.title: Stage Config Files
item.description:
If you only wish to override or provide new Xresources values, staging configs is not required and not recommended. Overriding Xresources value is described in a separate article.

Regolith uses a number of configuration files to determine the behavior and look of various components. While it’s possible to simply edit these files directly, users who do so run the risk of having their configurations overwritten upon future updates. The Debian packaging system should ask users if they wish to take updates or keep the existing files, but this may have unintended side effects if users take partial updates of files. As such Regolith, upon login, will look for user-staged version of configuration files and load those instead of the defaults if they exist. This is recommended over editing the files directly as it gives the user more control over their configuration. This page describes how to create these files.

Depending on what you wish to change, you may need your own copy of the window manager config file: the i3 config file in the X11 session, or the sway config file in the Wayland session. If you’re looking to change the way Regolith looks, Xresources may be all you need. If you want to update or add keybindings or swap out components, you’ll most likely need to stage the config file.

A staged copy replaces the default file completely, so changes that later Regolith updates make to the default file don’t reach you. To add or change a few settings, a config partial in ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config.d/ (X11) or ~/.config/regolith3/sway/config.d/ (Wayland) is often enough. See Customize i3 Configuration.

i3 Config (X11 Session)

  1. Copy the default Regolith i3 config file into your home directory:
mkdir -p ~/.config/regolith3/i3
cp /etc/regolith/i3/config ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config
  1. Log out and back in. The Regolith session will automatically detect and load your user-staged file.

Verify the Change

  1. Verify by running i3 --moreversion and noting the config file that is printed as a result. It should be the copy you just created. If not, be sure the path is correct. It must exactly be ~/.config/regolith3/i3/config for Regolith to load it.

Sway Config (Wayland Session)

  1. Copy the default Regolith sway config file into your home directory:
mkdir -p ~/.config/regolith3/sway
cp /etc/regolith/sway/config ~/.config/regolith3/sway/config
  1. Log out and back in. The Regolith session will automatically detect and load your user-staged file.

Verify the Change

  1. Verify by running pgrep -a -x sway. The output shows the config file sway was started with, for example sway -c /home/user/.config/regolith3/sway/config. It should be the copy you just created. If not, be sure the path is correct. It must exactly be ~/.config/regolith3/sway/config for Regolith to load it.

item.title: Support Multiple Batteries
item.description:
Out of the box the bar shows the combined charge of all batteries: in the X11 session once the i3xrocks-battery package is installed, and in the Wayland session by default. For some laptops that have multiple batteries, e.g. ThinkPads, you may want to have each battery displayed.

i3

  1. Install the battery blocklet if it is not installed yet:
sudo apt install i3xrocks-battery
  1. Stage your i3xrocks configuration files, including 80_battery, then open ~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d/80_battery in your editor of choice. Once ~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d contains files, the bar shows only the blocklets in that directory, so copy every blocklet you want to keep.
  2. Find the line that pertains to the battery blocklet:
~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d/80_battery
# Battery indicator
#
# Displays total percentage charge left of specified battery.
# You can specify the instance by adding:
# instance=BAT0
[battery]
interval=10
  1. List all the batteries on your machine by running:
upower --enumerate

# /org/freedesktop/UPower/devices/line_power_AC
# /org/freedesktop/UPower/devices/battery_BAT0
# /org/freedesktop/UPower/devices/battery_BAT1
# /org/freedesktop/UPower/devices/DisplayDevice
  1. Update the staged config file to have one blocklet per battery, using the UPower device names (battery_BAT0, battery_BAT1) as the instance:
~/.config/regolith3/i3xrocks/conf.d/80_battery
...
# Battery indicator
#
# Displays total percentage charge left of specified battery.
[battery]
interval=10
instance=battery_BAT0

[battery]
interval=10
instance=battery_BAT1
  1. Refresh the bar:
regolith-look refresh

Sway

  1. Stage your i3status-rust config file:
mkdir -p ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust
cp /etc/regolith/i3status-rust/config.toml ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml
  1. Configure to supply i3status-rust with your config file:
echo "wm.bar.status_config: ~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml" >> ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources
  1. List all the battery instances running on your machine by running:
ls /sys/class/power_supply/

# AC BAT0 BAT1
  1. In the staged config file, replace the battery block (which shows the combined charge, device = "DisplayDevice") with one block per battery:
~/.config/regolith3/i3status-rust/config.toml
[[block]]
block = "battery"
interval = 10
device = "BAT0"

[[block]]
block = "battery"
interval = 10
device = "BAT1"
  1. Refresh the session, or log back in:
regolith-look refresh

See the i3status-rust battery block documentation for further options.

Further Reading

See the reference page for configurations for more details about config files in Regolith.

item.title: Test What's New in Regolith 3.5
item.description:
This page lists the changes from Regolith 3.4 to 3.5 that you can see or feel in normal use, with the steps to try each one yourself. Internal fixes (packaging, build, quoting and the like) are left out.

Regolith 3.5 is available for Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04, 25.10 and 26.04, and Debian 12 and 13. To install it, follow the installation instructions. To upgrade from Regolith 3.4, see Upgrade from Regolith 3.4 in the release notes. Debian 12 has the X11 session only, so the Wayland items don’t apply there.

Each item says:

  • what changed, and which session it applies to: X11 (“Regolith / X11”, i3) or Wayland (“Regolith / Wayland”, sway);
  • Parity when the feature worked in only one session in 3.4 and now works in both;
  • the package that carries it, with the version that Regolith 3.5 ships, and the pull request;
  • how to try it, and what you should see.

Before you begin

Check that you have Regolith 3.5

In a terminal (super enter):

cat /etc/regolith/version
apt policy regolith-desktop | head -4

You should see REGOLITH_VERSION=3.5, and Installed: 4.11.0-1regolith-<codename> (or later) with the same Candidate version, where <codename> is your release, such as noble or trixie. If the candidate is newer, run sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade first.

To see the versions of the packages that the items below refer to:

dpkg-query -W regolith-wm-config regolith-avizo regolith-powerd regolith-displayd regolith-inputd regolith-session-common ilia i3status-rs regolith-i3xrocks-config regolith-control-center sway-regolith regolith-look-default

Switch sessions

Most items name a session. To change session:

  1. Log out: press super shift e, then Log Out (X11) or Logout (Wayland).
  2. On the login screen, click your name, then the gear icon at the bottom right.
  3. Pick Regolith / X11 or Regolith / Wayland, and type your password.

In a terminal, echo $XDG_SESSION_TYPE prints x11 or wayland.

What you need

Most checks need only a keyboard and a mouse. A few need hardware: a laptop for the brightness keys and the battery warning, a USB stick for automount, and a second monitor for the monitor labels. Some steps install a package or change a setting; each says how to undo it if it isn’t obvious.

Session parity at a glance

These features worked in only one session in Regolith 3.4. In 3.5 they work in both.

Feature 3.4 3.5
Volume indicator, 1.5 s timeout, 100% limit, fine volume steps X11 both
Brightness keys on the lock screen X11 both
Calculator and Home Folder keys X11 both
Print screenshot keys X11 both
Super+Print screenshot keys Wayland both
Screen Blank settings, screen off after locking, apps that lock the screen X11 both
Logout and power off requests ask first X11 both
Automount, low-battery warning X11 both
“Keep these display settings?”, monitor labels X11 both
Compose key, key repeat, system keyboard layout on first login X11 both
Background from Settings, theme of X11 apps, look wallpaper colours X11 both
CPU block, 12/24-hour clock on the bar X11 both
Gap keys, Terminate App X11 both
Next Free Workspace keys, dialogs in the window switcher Wayland both

Volume, brightness and media keys

Volume indicator on every key press

Wayland · Parity · regolith-avizo 0.1.8 · avizo#6

On Ubuntu 26.04 the volume keys changed the volume without showing the on-screen indicator, unless the sound was muted.

  1. Press volume up, then volume down.

You should see: a box in the middle of the screen with a speaker icon and a level bar, on every press. The volume block on the bar follows.

The indicator goes away after 1.5 seconds

Wayland · Parity · regolith-avizo 0.1.8 · avizo#8, Discussion #1107

The indicator used to stay on screen for about 5 seconds. It now hides after 1.5 seconds, as in the X11 session.

  1. Press volume up once and count.

You should see: the indicator disappear between one and two seconds after the key press. You can set another time with time = in ~/.config/avizo/config.ini.

Volume keys stop at 100%

Wayland · Parity · regolith-avizo 0.1.8 · avizo#9

The volume keys used to raise the volume past 100% without limit.

  1. Set the volume close to the top: pactl set-sink-volume @DEFAULT_SINK@ 97%
  2. Press volume up twice.
  3. Run pactl get-sink-volume @DEFAULT_SINK@.

You should see: 100%, not 105% or more.

Fine volume steps and modifier variants

Wayland · Parity · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#98

The modifier variants of the volume and player keys that the X11 session handles now work in sway too.

  1. Run pactl set-sink-volume @DEFAULT_SINK@ 50%.
  2. Press shift volume up, then ctrl volume up, then alt volume up, running pactl get-sink-volume @DEFAULT_SINK@ after each.
  3. Press alt mute twice.

You should see: 52% (Shift makes a fine 2% step), then 57% and 62% (Ctrl and Alt act like the plain key). alt mute mutes and unmutes.

Brightness keys on the lock screen

Wayland · Parity · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#74, fixes regolith-wm-config#73

On a laptop, the brightness keys did nothing while the screen was locked, so a screen dimmed all the way stayed dark.

  1. Press brightness up: the indicator shows a brightness icon and the level.
  2. Lock the screen with super escape.
  3. Press brightness down and brightness up.

You should see: the brightness change while the lock screen is up.

Sharp indicator on scaled displays

Wayland · regolith-avizo 0.1.8 · avizo#7

On a display with a scale above 100%, the indicator’s icons were blurry.

  1. Run swaymsg output '*' scale 2 (on a HiDPI display your scale may already be above 1).
  2. Press volume down.
  3. Run swaymsg output '*' scale 1 to go back.

You should see: a crisp speaker icon with sharp edges.

Calculator and Home Folder keys

Wayland · Parity · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#97

Keyboards with launcher keys can use them in sway as in the X11 session.

  1. Press the Calculator key.
  2. Press the Home Folder (Explorer) key.

You should see: GNOME Calculator (if it is installed, also as a snap), then Files.

Screenshots

Print screenshot keys in Wayland

Wayland · Parity · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#78

In 3.4, plain print did nothing in sway. It now has the same keys as the X11 session.

Key Result
print Saves the whole screen to ~/Pictures
shift print Drag an area with the mouse; saves it to ~/Pictures
alt print Saves the focused window to ~/Pictures
ctrl print, ctrl shift print, ctrl alt print The same, copied to the clipboard instead
  1. Press print and alt print, and run ls -t ~/Pictures | head -2.
  2. Press ctrl print and run wl-paste -l.

You should see: two new PNG files, then image/png in the clipboard. Each screenshot adds a notification (the bell count on the bar goes up; super n lists them). The older super print keys still work.

Super+Print screenshot keys in X11

X11 · Parity · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#96

The three screenshot keys that only the Wayland session had are now in the X11 session too.

Key Result
super print Copies the focused window to the clipboard
super shift print Click a window or drag an area; saves it to ~/Pictures and copies it
super shift ctrl print Saves all screens to ~/Pictures
  1. Press super print and run xclip -selection clipboard -t TARGETS -o | grep png.
  2. Press super shift print, click a window, and run ls -t ~/Pictures | head -1.

You should see: image/png, then a new Screenshot from …png with the size of that window, and a “Screenshot of anything” notification.

Lock screen, idle and power

Screen Blank follows Settings

Wayland · Parity · regolith-powerd 0.10.0 · regolith-powerd#24, regolith-powerd#44

sway now follows Settings › Power as the X11 session does. In 3.4, turning screen blanking off still blanked the screen after 5 seconds and locked it after 10, and the dim, blank and lock times didn’t match the settings.

  1. Open Settings (super c) › Power.
  2. Turn Automatic Screen Blank off, and leave the mouse and keyboard alone for two minutes.
  3. Turn it back on, set Delay to 1 minute, and leave the machine alone for a little over a minute.
  4. Set Delay back to your usual value.

You should see: with blanking off, the screen stays on and unlocked (it may dim). With 1 minute, the screen turns off and the session locks after one minute.

The screen turns off soon after you lock it

Wayland · Parity · regolith-powerd 0.10.0 · regolith-powerd#39

After super escape the lock screen used to stay lit until the normal idle timeout (more than 5 minutes).

  1. Lock with super escape, and don’t touch anything.
  2. Lock again, press a key to wake the lock screen, and wait.

You should see: the screen turn off about 5 seconds after locking, and 30 seconds after the last key press on the lock screen.

Apps and loginctl can lock the screen

Wayland · Parity · regolith-powerd 0.10.0 · regolith-powerd#25

sway now provides GNOME’s screen saver interface. Before, xdg-screensaver lock did nothing, and password managers that lock with the screen (KeePassXC, for example) stayed unlocked.

  1. Run loginctl lock-session, and unlock with your password.
  2. Run xdg-screensaver lock, and unlock.

You should see: the lock screen each time.

Switch keyboard layout on the lock screen

Wayland · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#63

With more than one input source (Settings › Keyboard › Add Input Source), you can now change the layout while the screen is locked, for example to type a password in another layout.

  1. Add a second input source, such as German.
  2. Lock with super escape and press super alt backspace.
  3. Unlock, and run swaymsg -t get_inputs | grep -m1 xkb_active_layout_name.

You should see: the second layout (here "German"). Press super alt backspace again to go back.

Logout and power off requests ask first

Wayland · Parity · regolith-powerd 0.10.0 · regolith-powerd#27

Logout, restart and power off requests from applications or the command line used to do nothing in sway.

  1. Run gnome-session-quit --logout in a terminal.

You should see: a yellow bar at the top: “Do you really want to logout? You will be logged out automatically in 60 seconds.” Click X to cancel. Logout, or waiting 60 seconds, logs you out.

USB sticks mount automatically

Wayland · Parity · regolith-powerd 0.10.0 · regolith-powerd#30

Plug in a USB stick or an SD card.

You should see: it is mounted under /run/media/$USER/ and opens in Files, as in the X11 session (findmnt /run/media/$USER/* lists it). This follows GNOME’s org.gnome.desktop.media-handling settings.

Low-battery warning and automatic Power Saver

Wayland · Parity · regolith-powerd 0.10.0 · regolith-powerd#23, fixes regolith-desktop#355; regolith-powerd#38

On a laptop, unplug the charger and let the battery run down to the low level (about 10%).

You should see: a “Power — Low Battery — 9% battery remaining” notification (with your percentage) (super n), and powerprofilesctl get switch from balanced to power-saver. When you plug the charger back in, the profile goes back to balanced.

No more crash reports from the audio idle inhibitor on X11

X11 · sway-audio-idle-inhibit 2.0.5 · SwayAudioIdleInhibit#9

The Wayland session’s audio idle inhibitor also started in the X11 session, where it crashed and caused “System program problem detected” dialogs.

  1. In the X11 session, run systemctl --user is-active sway-audio-idle-inhibit.
  2. In the Wayland session, run it again.

You should see: inactive on X11 and active on Wayland.

Displays

Keep these display settings?

Wayland · Parity · regolith-displayd 0.6.0 · regolith-displayd#28, fixes regolith-displayd#15

A display change from Settings now asks for confirmation, and goes back by itself if you don’t confirm, so a wrong mode can’t leave you with a black screen.

  1. Open Settings (super c) › Displays.
  2. Change Scale (for example to 125%), and click Apply.
  3. Don’t press anything for 20 seconds.

You should see: “Keep these display settings? Settings changes will revert in … seconds”, counting down from 20, with “Enter: Keep Changes” and “Esc: Revert Settings”. After 20 seconds the old scale comes back. Press enter instead to keep the change.

Monitor numbers on screen

Wayland · Parity · regolith-displayd 0.6.0, regolith-powerd 0.10.0 · regolith-displayd#18, regolith-powerd#28, fixes regolith-displayd#16; regolith-displayd#22

With two or more monitors, open Settings (super c) › Displays.

You should see: a number in the top left corner of each monitor, matching the numbers in the panel. The panel names each monitor by maker and size, as in the X11 session.

Keyboard and input

Compose key and other keyboard options

Wayland · Parity · regolith-inputd 0.6.1 · regolith-inputd#12, fixes regolith-inputd#6

  1. Open Settings (super c) › Keyboard › Compose Key, turn it on and choose Right Alt.
  2. In a terminal, press and release right alt, then type o c; then right alt, ', e.

You should see: © and é. In 3.4 the setting had no effect in sway.

Key repeat settings

Wayland · Parity · regolith-inputd 0.6.1 · regolith-inputd#14

The repeat settings now apply when you log in, and turning repeat off works.

  1. Open Settings › Accessibility › Typing, turn Repeat Keys off, and run swaymsg -t get_inputs | grep -m1 repeat_rate: it prints "repeat_rate": 0. Turn it back on.
  2. Run gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.keyboard delay 250, log out and in again, and run swaymsg -t get_inputs | grep -m1 repeat_delay.
  3. Run gsettings reset org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.keyboard delay to go back.

You should see: "repeat_delay": 250 after the new login.

A new account gets the system keyboard layout

Wayland · Parity · regolith-session 1.3.1 · regolith-session#78

A user whose first login was “Regolith / Wayland” got the US layout, whatever the system keyboard was set to.

  1. On a system whose keyboard layout isn’t US (localectl status shows it), create a user, and log in to Regolith / Wayland for the first time.

You should see: the system layout on the bar’s keyboard block (for example “French”).

Sticky keys, slow keys, bounce keys and mouse keys in sway

Wayland · sway-regolith 1.11.2 · sway-regolith#48

sway has new keyboard accessibility options. The toggles in Settings › Accessibility › Typing don’t reach sway yet, so set them with swaymsg or in your sway configuration.

  1. Run swaymsg input type:keyboard sticky_keys enabled.
  2. Press and release shift, then press a in a terminal.
  3. Run swaymsg input type:keyboard sticky_keys disabled.

You should see: A. swaymsg -t get_inputs | grep -m1 sticky_keys shows the state; man sway-input lists slow_keys, bounce_keys and mouse_keys.

Bar

The Wayland bar shows the same blocks

Wayland · Parity · i3status-rs 0.40.0-4 · i3status-rs_debian#25

The sway bar has a CPU block, as the X11 bar has, and no longer shows an empty red battery on machines without a battery.

You should see: a CPU percentage between the network and disk blocks, and a battery block only on a laptop.

The Wayland clock follows the time format

Wayland · Parity · i3status-rs 0.40.0-4 · i3status-rs_debian#26

  1. In the evening, run gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface clock-format 12h (the Time Format setting of Settings › System › Date & Time).
  2. Wait 5 seconds, then run gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface clock-format 24h.

You should see: the bar’s clock change from 24-hour time (20:05) to 12-hour time (08:05) and back, without restarting anything.

AM and PM on the X11 clock

X11 · regolith-i3xrocks-config 6.0.1 · regolith-i3xrocks-config#170

  1. Run gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface clock-format 12h, then press super shift r.

You should see: the time with AM or PM, for example 09:04 PM.

Volume and microphone blocks on PipeWire

X11 · Parity · regolith-i3xrocks-config 6.0.1 · regolith-i3xrocks-config#161, regolith-i3xrocks-config#167, fixes regolith-desktop#1087; regolith-i3xrocks-config#175

The X11 volume and microphone blocks showed no level on PipeWire, the default on Ubuntu.

  1. Install the blocks if you don’t have them: sudo apt install i3xrocks-volume i3xrocks-microphone, then press super shift r.
  2. Scroll up over the volume block until it stops.

You should see: a speaker and a microphone with their levels. Scrolling stops at 100%.

The CPU block turns red under load and opens System Monitor

X11 · regolith-i3xrocks-config 6.0.1 · regolith-i3xrocks-config#168, regolith-i3xrocks-config#171

  1. Load every CPU for 15 seconds: for i in $(seq $(nproc)); do timeout 15 sh -c 'while :; do :; done' & done
  2. Click the CPU block.

You should see: the CPU value in red while the load runs (it turns to the warning colour from 50% and to red from 80%). The click opens System Monitor in a floating window.

Launcher (ilia)

All of these are in ilia 0.20.1 and work in both sessions. Open the launcher with super space.

Search with several words, in any order

X11 and Wayland · ilia#128, fixes ilia#77; ilia#151

  1. Type monitor system.
  2. Clear it and type editor text.

You should see: System Monitor, then Vim (found by its generic name “Text Editor”). Each word must match, in any order, in the name, generic name or keywords.

Home and End

X11 and Wayland · ilia#129, fixes ilia#36

Press end, then home.

You should see: the last row selected, then the first.

Run a command that isn’t in the list

X11 and Wayland · ilia#127, fixes ilia#3

  1. Open the command launcher with super shift space.
  2. Type touch /tmp/ilia-test and press enter.
  3. Run ls /tmp/ilia-test.

You should see: the file exists. In 3.4, Enter did nothing when the text matched no item.

Terminal applications open in a terminal

X11 and Wayland · ilia#131, fixes ilia#92

Type htop and press enter.

You should see: the program running in a terminal window.

Newest notification first, and Delete removes one

X11 and Wayland · ilia#132, fixes regolith-desktop#607; ilia#137

  1. Run notify-send first-note; sleep 1; notify-send second-note.
  2. Open the notifications with super n, and press delete.

You should see: second-note at the top and highlighted; after Delete only first-note is left, highlighted.

Right Super closes, keypad Enter launches

X11 and Wayland · ilia#155, ilia#136

  1. Open the launcher and press the right super key.
  2. Open it again, type calc, and press enter on the numeric keypad.

You should see: the launcher closes, as with the left Super key; then Calculator starts.

Run a key binding from the keybinding viewer

X11 and Wayland · ilia#158, ilia#159, ilia#161

  1. Open the keybinding viewer with super shift ?.
  2. Type terminal, and press enter on “Launch - Terminal”.

You should see: a new terminal window.

Dialogs in the window switcher on X11

X11 · Parity · ilia#147

  1. Run zenity --question --title=test-dialog --text=hello &.
  2. Open the window switcher with super ctrl space.

You should see: test-dialog in the list, as in the Wayland session. In 3.4 the X11 list left dialog windows out.

Windows and workspaces

Switch back to the previous workspace

X11 and Wayland · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#80, fixes regolith-desktop#591

  1. On workspace 1, press super 3.
  2. Press super alt tab twice.

You should see: workspace 1, then 3 again. The key is wm.binding.ws_back_and_forth.

Resize mode arrows go the right way

X11 and Wayland · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#87

  1. Open two terminals one above the other: super enter, super v, super enter.
  2. Press super r, then up a few times, then escape.

You should see: the focused window grow taller with up and shorter with down, like k and j. In 3.4 the arrows did the opposite.

Gap keys in Wayland

Wayland · Parity · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#92

  1. Open two windows side by side.
  2. Press super =, then super shift =, then super minus and super shift minus.

You should see: the gaps between the windows grow, grow more, and shrink back.

Terminate App in Wayland

Wayland · Parity · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#70

Focus a terminal (foot, a native Wayland app) and press super alt q.

You should see: the window is killed. In 3.4 this key only worked on X11 apps.

Next Free Workspace keys in X11

X11 · Parity · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#71

With a window open on workspace 1, press super `.

You should see: the first empty workspace. super shift ` moves the focused window to it, and super alt ` takes the window and follows it.

Swapping Super and Alt works

X11 and Wayland · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#63, fixes regolith-desktop#504, regolith-desktop#1098

  1. Add wm.mod: Mod1 and wm.alt: Mod4 to ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources, and press super shift r.
  2. Press alt 3, then alt 1.
  3. Remove the two lines and press alt shift r.

You should see: no configuration error bar, and Alt switching workspaces.

Looks and appearance

Dark looks reach GTK 4 apps

X11 and Wayland · regolith-look-default 0.9.0, regolith-look-extra 0.11.0 · regolith-look-default#9, regolith-look-default#10, regolith-look-extra#25, fixes regolith-look-extra#19

Every look now sets GNOME’s light or dark style, so GTK 4 and libadwaita apps follow it.

  1. Run gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.interface color-scheme.
  2. Open Settings (super c) or Calculator.

You should see: 'prefer-dark' with the default look, and dark windows. Settings › Appearance shows Dark selected.

Settings sets the Wayland wallpaper

Wayland · Parity · regolith-control-center 1.50.5 · regolith-control-center#31

  1. Open Settings (super c) › Appearance, scroll to Background, and click a picture.
  2. Lock the screen with super escape.

You should see: the picture as the desktop background right away, and on the lock screen. It is saved in ~/.config/regolith3/Xresources (regolith.wallpaper.file); remove those lines and press super shift r to go back to the look’s wallpaper.

X11 apps follow the theme in Wayland

Wayland · Parity · regolith-wm-config 4.13.1 · regolith-wm-config#69

Apps that run under XWayland used to get the default light theme, fonts and cursor.

  1. Run GDK_BACKEND=x11 nm-connection-editor.

You should see: the window in the same theme and font as native apps (dark with the default look).

Look wallpaper colours and gradients in Wayland
